The local HTTP API server ships its own API documentation and a single method-dispatch endpoint: "By default, api documentation is available at http://127.0.0.1:12315/."; "POST `/api` - `method` can be any of the ones listed in https://plugins-doc.logseq.com/. `args` is an array of arguments to pass to method."; "Supports CORS for use from another web page or a browser extension." Auth is a user-created bearer token (worked curl examples: "curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:12315/api -H \"Authorization: Bearer {replace with your-token-value-here}\""). No OpenAPI document, sandbox, or versioning policy is published.

New user coming from Bear and Obsidian: Logseq fits a workflow of increasingly nested lists. The 'turn this block into its own page' command made the tool click and solves lists getting too deeply nested.
Two main problems: Logseq wasn't designed from the ground up to prevent data loss and has had data-loss issues. Still, the user knows of no other good local-first outliner like Workflowy.

Loves Logseq: the embedded PDF reader is quite good, and adding comments directly as blocks is amazing. Queries are still hard for beginners and less flexible than TiddlyWiki. Support for ordinary checkboxes (not TODO items) is surprisingly limited.

Logseq is my new favourite outliner, but indexing and responsiveness slow down massively once you have a few million words. You have to break data into many smaller notes. Putting up with it because it's improving and open source.
Has used Logseq near-daily for 7 months; poor performance is the main gripe. Even on an M1 there is very noticeable lag navigating between pages. Would gladly pay a subscription to fix it.
Became a $15/month sponsor to try Logseq's own sync in testing. It works but has enough bugs that they wouldn't rely on it yet. The team is responsive to fixing reported bugs.

Uses Syncthing with Logseq and is pretty happy, but you must be careful running multiple Logseq instances at once and re-index often. Another user syncing via a shared iCloud folder says it works OK with occasional data loss.
Uses Logseq personally and for work almost daily for about a year. Calls it the 'least bad' PKM platform: no mandatory subscription, local data, and source availability.
Highlighting and annotating PDFs in Logseq connects them with all my other notes; I built a scan→OCR→import pipeline. I wish it did the same for epubs, which I read far more.

Has used Logseq for a couple of months coming from Roam and prefers local markdown files. However, the official Advanced Query documentation is bleak; most useful tips came from random gists and forum posts.
The strong focus on bullet points made long-form text cumbersome. Pasting turns newlines into lists, and performance on blocks of text was so bad it died when pasting a few paragraphs.
Logseq's journalling and time-tracking is a beauty. But on a PKM shared with other tools it strips blank lines and converts top-level items to bullets, so this user always returns to Obsidian.

With ADHD traits, the user finds Obsidian overwhelming. Logseq's ability to focus on a single bullet helps them re-orient, and list manipulation with many keyboard/mouse shortcuts feels better than in Obsidian.
Logseq lost me as a daily user: Obsidian 1.0 now has plugins for almost everything I used Logseq for, without the incessant bugs. It shouldn't take a year to clean up cursor movement.

Too little, too late: Logseq remained a buggy mess on an unmaintained Electron. After years of stagnation, the new database format means data can no longer be kept as markdown files, which doesn't work with Claude edits and version control.
Still uses Logseq, which conceptually fits how my brain works. But it's been dormant for years and early sync attempts didn't work well; I paid to support sync and saw nothing for years.

Loved Logseq's UI/UX and donated monthly, but lost faith after apparent stagnation and went back to Org-mode. The interface was slow and buggy, and both the Org and Markdown backends are non-standard.

Has used Logseq DB nightly for a year: a great concept, very fast and easy to learn. Tagging blocks makes them typed things (project, author, quote). Some concepts (Assets, Library) are still half-baked, but they take and retrieve more notes.

Happy Logseq user since summer, using it as a personal and work knowledge base. Appreciates the publishing features and GitHub sync; self-hosting knowledge graphs for their team works well and intuitively despite early hiccups.

Tried Roam but dropped it to keep control of their data (and over price). With Logseq on a git repo, they haven't opened Emacs since and can still clone for org-agenda: 'blown away... checks every box.'
